activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Jake was getting better from his cold. He sat on his bed with a box of tissues. His nose was runny. He pulled out a soft tissue. Then he blew his nose. Toot! He dropped the tissue on the floor.

Mom came in. She picked up the tissue. "Used tissues go in the bin," she said. She pointed at the little bin by the door. Jake looked at the bin. Could he get a tissue in from far away? He wanted to try.

Jake blew his nose again. He held the tissue up high. He aimed. He dropped it. It fell in! "Yay!" said Jake. He laughed and clapped. His shy little cat peeked out from under the bed. Then Jake blew his nose once more. He fixed his aim and dropped the tissue. In it went. Mom smiled and said, "Good shot, Jake."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Grayson put on Papa's big boot. It went clomp, clomp on the floor. "I am a giant!" he said. His teddy bear was the giant's baby. Grayson made soup for the baby in the pretend kitchen. He stirred it with a spoon. The pot went crash. Cups rolled under the table. Plates sat upside down on the rug.

Then Grayson could not find the red spoon. "Where did it go?" he asked. Papa peeked under the chair. "Here it is," said Papa. Grayson reached for it. But wait. The kitchen was a big mess. He could not cook more giant soup here.

So Grayson put each cup back on the shelf. The plates went into the little sink. The pot went on the stove, all alone. "All clean," said Grayson. Then he spelled out his bear's name, B-E-A-R, and tucked the baby into bed. "Night night," said Grayson. "Sleep tight, little bear."

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name.

"First you hold it like this," said the woman. She was his mama. She showed him how to hold the pencil. Gabriel tried it too.

He made a G. He made an A. Then he made a big wobbly B. It leaned over like a sleepy duck. Gabriel frowned. "My B is all wrong," he said.

"Try the pink eraser," said Mama. Gabriel turned the pencil around. He rubbed the wobbly B. He rubbed and rubbed. The wobbly B was gone! The paper was clean again.

"Now I can try again," said Gabriel. He held the pencil tight. He made a new B. It stood up tall. He made R, I, E, L.

"Look, Mama! GABRIEL!" he shouted. He jumped up and did a happy stomp. Then he sat back down. "Now I want to write it big!"

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Bennett stood in the music room. Miss Rosa played a song on the piano. All the children clapped. Bennett clapped too, fast like rain. But his claps did not match the song. The song went slow and steady. His claps went all over.

Miss Rosa stopped playing. "Listen first," she said. "Clapping along to the beat means clapping at the same time as the beat of the music." Bennett put his hands in his lap. He listened to the big slow beat. One, two, one, two.

Then he clapped when the beat went. His hands landed right on time. "I did it!" he said. Mia smiled at him. She had been hiding her hands behind her yellow skirt because she was shy. Bennett reached over and showed her the beat with his hand. She clapped too. Then they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle" together, all the way from the start to the end, with no help at all. Miss Rosa played louder, and after music time she gave everyone warm cups of milk.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Oliver sat at the dinner table. He kicked his feet under his chair. One brown sock fell off his foot. It landed on the floor.

"One sock," said Oliver. He counted it. "One."

Mama came over. "A sock needs its partner," she said. "A pair means two, like a pair of socks."

Oliver looked under the table. He saw his brown foot. He saw the sock on the floor. He counted again. "One, two, three," he said, pointing at the chair legs. "Four, five, six." He kept going slow. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Can you fetch the sock?" asked Mama.

"I can fetch it," said Oliver. He climbed down. He picked up the sock. He looked for the other one. He looked left. He looked right. There it was, under his high chair.

He pulled it out. He put on one sock. He put on the other sock.

"Now I have a pair," said Oliver. "Two socks!"

Mama smiled. "Two socks for two feet," she said.

Oliver wiggled his toes. Both socks were on. He sat back down at the table. He tapped his socks together. "One, two," he said. "A pair."

story:
Evan was playing in the backyard. He had a big box of blocks. He wanted to build a tower on his little desk. But first, he wanted to sort them.

Evan picked up a red block. "Red," he said. He put it in a pile. Then a blue block. Then another red block. "One red, two red, three red," he said. His red pile grew tall. The blue pile grew too. Now all the blocks were sorted by color.

Then his big sister Mia came out. "I can sort them a different way," she said. She put all the big blocks in one pile. She put all the little blocks in another pile. Evan's mouth fell open. The same blocks! Now they were sorted by size!

"Let me try," said Evan. He found some round blocks. He put them in one pile. He put the square blocks in another pile. "Sorted by shape!" he said. Mia clapped. Then they built one big tower together. It was Evan's favorite kind of tower, red and blue, big and little, round and square, all the way up to the sky.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Isabelle went to the farm with Grandpa. She wanted to learn her five senses. Grandpa said, "Let's find them one by one."

First Isabelle saw a shiny red apple on a tree. "I used my eyes," she said. Then she touched a soft sheep. "I used my hands." Next she heard a loud cow. "Moo! I used my ears." She smelled bread. Grandpa was going to bake it later. "I used my nose," she said. "One sense left," said Grandpa.

Grandpa picked two apples. One was sweet. One was sour. "Guess with your tongue," he said. Isabelle took a little bite of the first apple. "Sweet!" she said. Then she tried the other one. Her face went squinty. "Sour!" she said, and she laughed.

Grandpa gave her a small gift. It was a shiny apple for her pocket. "My tongue knew," said Isabelle. She patted her pocket all the way home.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Josephine wanted to build a big tower at daycare. She found a heavy box. She pulled it. She pushed it. It would not move. The box was too heavy for her.

Then she found a small pillow. It was light. She picked it up so easily. She put it on top of the box. It felt like a feather in her arms. Ben looked at the pillow and the box. "Heavy and light are opposites," he said. Josephine laughed and stacked three more pillows.

Outside, the big fire truck toy went fast down the hill. The little duck toy went slow. At snack time, Teacher Mia poured the hot soup. Josephine waited. It cooled slowly, and she blew on each small spoonful. Her spoon went fast when the soup was just right.

At pickup, Mama gave her a kiss. Josephine hugged the light pillow to her chest and waved goodbye to the big tower.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Alexis sat at the big table. His friend Milo came to dinner. Milo brought a little red car. It was heavy for such a small car.

Milo zoomed the car on the table. Alexis wanted a turn now. His hand went out fast. Grandma put her hand on his. "Milo is first," she said softly.

Alexis wanted to grab it. That felt hard. Grandma said, "Try three slow breaths." Alexis took one slow breath. Then two. Then three. His hand felt calm. Milo rolled the car to him. "Your turn," said Milo.

Alexis zoomed the car to Milo's cup. Then he rolled it back. They took turns, back and forth, all through dinner. After dinner, Alexis helped wash his hands at the sink. Water ran over his ear as he leaned down. He laughed and gave Milo one more turn with the red car.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jacob stood in the bathroom. He looked at his face in the mirror with his eyes. He saw a boy with toothpaste on his chin.

Then his nose knew something. A yummy smell came in under the door. "Sniff, sniff," said Jacob. "I smell dinner! Is it soup?" His tummy made a little growl. He did not want to miss one drop.

Daddy came to the door. "You smelled it before you saw it," said Daddy. "Good nose! Come and listen." Jacob used his ears. He heard the pot bubble on the stove. Daddy stirred it with a big spoon. The man in the kitchen was Daddy, and he was safe.

At the table, Jacob touched his warm bowl with his fingers. He took a taste with his tongue. "Soup!" said Jacob. "My nose was right." Daddy smiled and gave him bread. The kitchen smelled good, and Jacob was warm and happy. "More bread, please," said Jacob.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Ivy went to the library with Dad. There was a new tablet on the little table. Ivy wanted to draw a cat on it. But the screen was dark and still.

Dad showed her the small button on the side. "Press that," he said. Ivy pressed it. The screen lit up, bright and pretty. She pressed the drawing app. It opened with a pop. Ivy drew a cat with green ears. She drew summer sun, too. "Your cat looks silly," said Dad. "That is the plan," said Ivy.

Soon it was time to go. Ivy remembered the small button. She pressed it once. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the table. "All done," said Ivy. Dad gave her a big grin. "Bye-bye, green-eared cat," said Ivy.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Jaxon sat on the big red cushion. Dad put the game on TV. Aunt Mia and Grandpa came too. Popcorn jumped in the bowl, warm and salty.

The blue team ran and ran. The red team ran too. "The blue team runs more," said Jaxon. "They win!" Grandpa laughed. "Look at the score," he said. Jaxon stood up and looked. The red team had more points. The red team was winning!

Jaxon watched more. A red player kicked the ball. It went in the net. The red score went up by one. "The ball went in," Jaxon shouted. "Now the number is bigger!" He marched around the couch like a little turtle in a hurry, arms and legs going fast.

The game ended. The red team had more points at the end. The TV said the red team won. The blue team had run a lot, but that was not what counted. Jaxon held up the popcorn bowl like a prize. "More points means you win," he said. Grandpa clapped. Aunt Mia cheered. Dad said, "Snack time, everyone!" Jaxon ran to the kitchen, not lost at all, right behind him.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought warm bread and fresh butter. They bought a big carton of milk too. At the bread stand, a lady sliced the bread flat on a wooden board. Dad said, "I will teach you to butter toast today." Ezra said, "Can I do it all by myself?" Dad said, "Yes, you can."

They sat at a little table. Dad put butter on Ezra's knife-safe spoon. Ezra spread the butter. The butter made the toast shiny. "I did it!" said Ezra. Then Ezra tried to pour milk from the big carton. It was too heavy. Milk nearly spilled. "Why is it so hard?" Ezra asked. Dad said, "The carton is too big for your hands."

Dad poured some milk into a small jug. Ezra held the little jug. He tipped it slowly. Milk went into his cup. Not one drop spilled. Ezra poured more milk into Dad's cup too. "Small jug, small hands," said Ezra. He drank his milk and ate his toast down to the last flat crumb. "Can we get juice next time?" asked Ezra. Dad laughed and said, "Yes, and a small jug to pour it from."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leah went to the library with her mom. There was a playroom in the back. Leah wanted to find the toy box, but it was empty. "Where did all the toys go?" she asked.

Her friend Ben was putting toys away on the wrong shelf. He had put a ball next to the books. Leah picked it up. "A ball is a toy," she said. "It goes in the toy box." She dropped it in. Thump!

Ben found a doll under the chair. He handed it to Leah. Dolls are toys too. In it went. Then Leah saw blocks by the door. Blocks are toys. In they went, one by one. Soon the toy box was full.

But then Leah heard a funny sound. Something was snoring in the toy box! She peeked inside. A fat orange cat was asleep on the doll. The cat twitched its nose. Leah gave it a soft pat. "The cat is not a toy," she whispered. "But it can stay." The cat purred and purred.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Sienna wanted to make a paper sun at camp. She found red paper and yellow paper. She wanted to cut long points for the sun's rays.

She saw the big scissors on the table. The big scissors had sharp, shiny points. "Can I use those?" she asked.

Camp Leader Joe shook his head. "Those are for me," he said. "Here are your safety scissors. They have rounded tips. I will watch while you cut."

The safety scissors were small and blue. Sienna held them. Snip, snip, snip. The yellow paper fell into long strips. "I did it!" she said. "The scissors make the paper fall!"

"Snip, snip, snip," she sang. Soon the sun had many rays. But one ray was too long. It looked like a dirty old sock.

"You can rip it shorter," said Joe. Sienna pulled the paper. Riiiip! The ray was short now. She put all the rays in her bag to carry home.

Then Joe held up a surprise. "Look what I cut with the big scissors," he said. It was a tiny paper crown. "For the sun artist," he said.

Sienna put it on her head. "My sun is boss of the sky now," she said.

story:
Jasper wanted to sort his toys. He had a big problem. His toy box was all mixed up.

He put all the toy cars in one pile. He put all the stuffed animals in another pile. The animals were bear, bunny and duck. Then Jasper saw something silly. A banana sat with the toy cars!

"Guess what I found," he told his sister, Mia. "A banana with my cars."

Mia laughed. "That is the odd one out," she said. "It does not belong there."

Jasper picked up the banana with gentle hands. He carried it to the kitchen. He gave it to Dad for snack time. Dad cut it into little round slices.

Jasper ran back to his toys. All the cars were together now. Only cars. No bananas.

"Odd one out," said Jasper. "Found you."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Lea sat at the big art table. Her teacher, Miss Jo, put out paper stars, glitter, and a full bottle of glue. "I will make a crown," said Lea. Miss Jo smiled. "A crown for a queen," she said.

Lea counted her stars. One, two, three, four, five. She put glue on each star. She stuck them on a long paper strip. Then she grabbed the crown to try it on. The stars slid off. The paper ends slid apart too. Lea's lip wobbled. "My crown is broken," she said.

Miss Jo sat down next to her. "The glue is still wet," she said. "Wet glue needs time to dry. Then the pieces hold together." Lea sniffed the glue. It smelled funny and sharp. She touched one dot of glue with her finger. It felt cold and slippery. Miss Jo set the crown on the shelf. "Let's wait," she said.

Lea drew pictures while they waited. One sun. One cat. One baby in a stroller. Then Miss Jo said, "Touch it now." Lea poked the glue. It felt hard and dry. She picked up the crown. The stars stayed on. The ends stayed stuck. Lea put the crown on her head. "It worked," she said. Miss Jo clapped her hands. "A queen with a fine crown," she said.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ellie stood on her tiptoes at Grandma's house. The big challah bread sat on the table. Everyone was coming for dinner.

Grandpa picked up the bread. "Time for the Hamotzi," he said. Ellie wanted to say it too. She wanted it very much.

"I can do it," said Ellie. Grandpa smiled. "Let's practice," he said. They practiced under the big tree. They practiced in the kitchen. Ellie got mixed up. She tried again. She got mixed up a different way. "Keep trying," said Grandpa. So Ellie kept trying. Practice, practice, practice.

Now everyone sat down. Aunt Sara held the baby. Cousins wiggled in their seats. Grandma put the warm bread in Grandpa's hands. Grandpa looked at Ellie.

"You say it with me," he said.

Ellie took a big breath. She said the blessing. Grandpa's voice went up, and Ellie's voice went up too. Then both voices came down together. Everyone at the table said "Amen."

The bread was cut and passed around. Ellie took her piece and bit it. "I said the Hamotzi," she said. Grandma kissed the top of her head.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia sat in the family car. She held her favorite toy bunny. "Are we going to the doctor?" she asked. Mom smiled. "We are going to a special doctor," she said.

Sofia hurried out of the car. The office door said DENTIST. A kind man in a blue coat waved. "Hello, Sofia!" he said. "Open wide, please." Sofia opened her mouth. He looked and looked. But he did not look at her ears. He did not look at her toes. He only looked at her teeth!

"You only check teeth?" Sofia asked. The man laughed. "Yes! A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth." Then he gave her a little mirror. Sofia held it up. She saw her own teeth shine back. "Hello, teeth!" she said. "Nice to meet you!"

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Rehmat wanted to play a game with her brother Sam. Sam held up a big red ball. "Say the opposite word," he said. Rehmat pointed at a small blue cup. "Small!" she said. Sam laughed. "Yes! Big and small are opposites."

Then Sam ran fast around the rug. "Fast!" he shouted. Rehmat walked very slowly. "Slow," she said. Sam clapped. Rehmat felt grumpy because she got one wrong. She said "hot" for the sun, but Sam said "cold."

Mama came in with warm milk. She held the cup so Rehmat would not touch anything hot. "Your milk is warm," said Mama. "But ice is cold." Rehmat touched the cold window glass with one finger. Then she saw the letter A on her blocks. She put a big block by a small block.

"Opposites are two different words," said Sam. Rehmat held up a big block and a small block. "Big and small!" she said. Sam hugged her. Rehmat drank her warm milk and smiled.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to bake cookies for the whole family. Grandma said, "Yes! Let's bake."

Parker poured the sugar. He stirred the eggs. Grandma let him drop the dough onto the pan. The pan looked full and bumpy, like a nest of little round stones.

"Now the pan goes in the oven," said Grandma. Parker reached for the oven door. Grandma held his hand. "A grown-up is in charge of the hot oven," she said. "You can watch from here." Grandma slid the pan in all by herself. Parker sat on his blue stool and waited. Soon the kitchen smelled sweet.

Grandma pulled the pan out. The round dough had turned into real cookies! Parker saw that. The oven made them warm and done. "You waited so nicely," Grandma said. Parker carried the plate to the table. Mom took a bite and smiled. Dad took two. Parker pointed at the oven. "The oven did that," he said. Grandma laughed and gave him the biggest cookie.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Weston was in the backyard. He wanted to make soup for Bear. He found a round bucket and a small stick. He put in a pinecone, two leaves, and a little rock. Then he stirred and stirred. "Soup is ready!" he said.

He held the spoon up to his mouth. He tipped it in. "Stop right there," said Mom. She knelt down next to him. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth." Weston looked at the pinecone soup. He was sorry. He did not want a real pinecone in his tummy.

He tried again. He held the spoon near his lips and made a big slurp sound. "Sluuurp!" Nothing went in his mouth. Mom clapped. Bear got a sip too, right on his fuzzy nose. Then Weston set his soup on the square patio stone. He patted Bear's head and said, "All done. Time for naps."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Nova stood by the wooden table at the community hall. Big pots of soup sat at one end. Nova was hungry. She wanted to eat right now.

Grandma held Nova's hand. "First we say the blessing," Grandma said. "Then we eat." Everyone at the table held hands. They bowed their heads. Nova looked at the soup. She looked at the bread. When could she eat?

Grandma spoke softly. "We thank you for this food. We thank you for our family." Nova waited. She squeezed Grandma's hand. Still they did not eat. Then everyone said one word together. "Amen." Right after that, the spoons went up, and the bread began to pass down the table.

Nova ate her soup. It was warm and good. Then a lady brought out a present, a box of little cakes. "Ooh," said Nova. Before the cakes, everyone held hands again. Nova watched carefully this time. She waited for the soft words. She waited and waited. Then came the word. "Amen," said everyone, and Nova said it too. She reached for a cake, and Grandma smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Everett turned four today. He was at Grandma's house. The cake sat on the big table. Grandma put in four little candles. Then she lit them with a match. Everett watched from his chair.

"Now we sing," said Grandma. Everyone began to sing. "Happy birthday to Everett," they sang. His name was in the song! He hid his smiling face behind his hands. "Sing it again," he said. "Please sing it again."

So they sang it again. "Happy birthday to Everett." He peeked through his fingers. His name was in the song both times. He was not mad at all. He blew out the candles. Grandma cut the cake. Everyone clapped. Then Everett asked, "Can we drive home and sing it again in the car?" And Grandma laughed and said, "Yes, we can."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Elijah wanted to play hide-and-seek at school. But he could not find anyone to count for him.

Miss Kim smiled. "I will be the seeker," she said. "You go hide, Elijah."

Elijah hid behind the toy horse. It was big and brown. He made himself tiny behind it.

Then Mia said, "I want to seek too." Miss Kim said, "We both will."

Mia covered her eyes. She counted very fast. "One two three four five!"

Elijah peeked out. His shoes were showing! He pulled them in.

The other kids called out, "Too fast, Mia! Count slowly. We need time to hide."

Mia counted again, slow and soft. "One... two... three..." Elijah held his breath and froze like a stone. He heard grass sounds outside the window. He heard a buzzing bee.

"Eight... nine... ten. Ready or not!" Mia opened her eyes.

She found Ben first. Then she found Sam. But she walked right past the toy horse. Elijah waited, still as still.

Then his tummy giggled. He giggled too. "You found me!" he laughed.

"My turn next," said Elijah. "Everyone hide. I will count to ten, nice and slow." He covered his eyes. "One... two... three..."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Bennett ran in from Grandma's backyard. He wanted to stir the pancake batter. The bowl sat on the big kitchen table. It smelled sweet like vanilla.

"First, the sink," said Grandma. She pointed to it. "Cooks wash their hands with soap and water before they touch food." Bennett looked at his hands. They had dirt on them from digging. He went to the sink. Grandma turned on the water. It ran warm over his fingers. He rubbed the soap until it made white bubbles.

Then Grandma held the bowl for him. Bennett stirred the batter round and round. The flour and milk mixed into something smooth and tan. He dipped one finger in to taste it. Grandma laughed. "That batter has raw egg," she said. "No tasting yet."

Grandpa poured the batter into the pan. The pan was hot, so Bennett stood far away on his stool. Soon the batter bubbled in little dots. Grandpa flipped each pancake high. One went so high that Bennett felt dizzy watching it. It landed right back in the pan.

The pancakes came to the table warm and golden. Bennett ate three. Grandpa ate five. Grandma put one more on Bennett's plate, and it was shaped like a heart.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Audrey ran into the pharmacy on a sunny day. Today she would get a shot. She was very excited. Then she saw the big table in the little room. Her tummy felt funny.

"I don't want to sit up there," said Audrey. The table was too big. Her feet could not touch the floor. Mom sat down on the chair instead. "Come sit on my lap," said Mom. Audrey climbed up. Mom held her in a big hug.

The nurse came in with a tiny tray. "Ready?" she asked. "Ready!" said Audrey. Mom's arms were warm and snug. Audrey took a deep breath. "You can squeeze my hand," said Mom. Audrey squeezed. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was done!

"That was fast," said Audrey. "It did not hurt much." The nurse poured a little juice from a small cup for her. Audrey drank it all. Mom picked her up high. "What a big girl," said Mom. Audrey held up her bandage and showed the whole pharmacy.

"It's my bandage," she said. "See you next day!"

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Peyton sat at Grandma's big table. She had red paint and a fat brush. She painted a big red sun. Then she wanted to play outside. She left the brush in the paint cup.

The next day, Peyton came back to the room. She picked up her brush. The brush felt hard. It would not bend at all. "Oh no," said Peyton. "My brush is all stiff."

Grandma held the brush under the tap. The warm water was too hot, so Grandma turned it to cool. She let Peyton watch. They put the brush in the water and swished it. The red paint came out. The brush turned soft again.

"Now we know," said Grandma. "After painting, we rinse the brush." Peyton got a fresh cup of water. She painted a blue fish. Then she rinsed her brush right away. The brush stayed soft.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jaxson sat at the dinner table. Daddy set down a big pot. It was soup night!

Jaxson felt excited. He loved soup night. He tapped his spoon on his bowl. Tap, tap, tap!

His sister Mia sat next to him. She covered her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked sad.

Jaxson stopped tapping. He looked at his spoon. Then he looked at Mia. Hmm, could they feel different about the same sound?

"I love the tap," Jaxson said. "You don't like it?"

"No," said Mia. "It scares me."

Daddy smiled. "Maybe you two like different things."

Jaxson put his spoon down. He wanted Mia to feel happy. He picked up his doll from the chair. "Want to feed the doll?" he asked.

Mia smiled big. "Yes!" She held the doll and made it dance over the bowl. The doll dipped in the air. Mia laughed and laughed.

"Slurp, slurp," said the doll. Now Mia was happy too.

Jaxson watched her. Same table, same soup. But he loved the tapping, and she loved the doll. He wondered what else they might like differently.

"Mia," he said, "do you like carrots?"

"No!" said Mia, with a grumpy face.

"I love carrots!" said Jaxson. He took a big bite.

Mia giggled and fed the doll one more slurp.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Rowan went to the big hall with Mama and Grandma. There were red lanterns on the walls. There was music and lots of people. Rowan held Mama's hand tight.

A girl named Mei walked up to Rowan. She was holding a small red envelope. "Look," said Mei. "It is for Lunar New Year. Many children get red envelopes. There is money inside." Rowan looked at the envelope. It was shiny and flat.

Then Grandma gave Rowan a red envelope too. Rowan wanted to open it right away. His fingers pulled at the corner. Mei shook her head. "Say thank you first," she said. Rowan stopped. He looked up at Grandma. "Thank you, Grandma," he said. Grandma smiled big. "You are welcome, Rowan." Then Rowan opened the envelope. Inside was a shiny coin. It caught the light and glowed.

At the table, Daddy poured warm tea for everyone. Rowan took one small cookie from the plate. The lanterns swayed above them. Mei waved from across the room. Rowan held up his coin so she could see it shine.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Audrey sat in the school library. She wanted to write her name. She found a card with the letter K on it. The K was bumpy. She could feel it with her finger.

Audrey picked up her pencil. She tried to write a K. She wrote it the wrong way. The legs went the wrong side. She rubbed it out with her arm and tried again. It came out wrong again. Audrey felt stuck.

She put her pencil down. Then she traced the bumpy K with her finger. Up, down, out. Up, down, out. She did it again and again. Then she picked up her pencil. She wrote a K. This time it was right! Audrey clapped her hands.

"Look!" she said to the teacher. "I can do it!" She wrote A, U, D, and then a big, happy K.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sadie ran to the playground with her dad. The sun was out and the slide was hot. "Careful, it is hot," Dad said. He put his hand on the slide first. Sadie touched it after, just a little. It felt warm like tea. She waited for the shady side to play on.

Then Sadie saw a boy on a bike. He zoomed down the path. He wore a big helmet on his head. Sadie wanted to ride her bike too. She ran to it and jumped on. "Wait," Dad said. "Where is your helmet?" Sadie stopped. She looked at the boy again. He had his helmet on his head.

Sadie walked back to the car. Her helmet sat inside. It was red with a star. She put it on. It felt snug over her nose strap. Then she pedaled off down the path. Her ride was short and fun. A dog ran beside her, and its ears flapped up and down.

Sadie rode past the swings. She stopped by Dad. "I had my helmet," she said. Dad smiled and held up a water bottle. The water was cold on Sadie's tongue. The boy on the bike rode by again. He waved, and Sadie waved back. "Race you to the tree," he called.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Aubrey stood in the school computer lab. Her teacher said, "We will use the tablets today." Aubrey looked at the little shelf. The tablets sat in a row, one, two, three.

"Press the round button," said her teacher. Aubrey pressed it. The screen lit up. She pressed it again. The picture came back. "I made it wake up!" she said.

She tapped the drawing app. She picked blue. Then she picked yellow. The two colors mixed on the screen. Blue and yellow made green. "One, two, three colors!" said Aubrey. She drew a big green frog.

Then it was time to go. Aubrey set her tablet on the soft couch. Ben came running. He was going to sit down. "Stop!" said the teacher. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place." Aubrey picked it up fast. She carried it to the shelf. One, two, three tablets in a row again. "My frog can rest here," said Aubrey. She patted the shelf and skipped to the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Alexander wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. Mom was cooking noodles on the stove. The kitchen was warm and sunny. Alexander tiptoed closer to peek inside. The pot made a cloud of steam. It went up, up, up. Alexander put his hand near the steam. Mom caught his hand right away. "Steam is hot," she said. "It can burn. Stay back." Alexander stepped back three big steps. He held Mom's apron and stayed close.

From far away, he still could see the bubbles. They popped and jumped in the water. Alexander clapped his hands. He saw the steam touch the sunny window. The window got foggy and wet. One little bubble went pop very loud. Alexander laughed. Then he ran to get his pencil. He drew the bubbles and the steam cloud on paper.

Dad came in and looked at the drawing. "You drew the steam too!" Dad said. Alexander pointed at the foggy window. The steam mark was still there. Dad gave him a high five. "Can I watch again tomorrow?" Alexander asked. Mom smiled and said, "Yes, from three big steps back." Alexander nodded. He held up his drawing so everyone could see the big steam cloud.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Josephine ran into the library with her mama. She wanted the counting book with the big red cover. "It is here somewhere," she said. A lady sang in the story room. "One, two, three, four, five," she sang. Josephine tapped her toes to it.

Then Josephine saw a door. A big number sat on the door. The number looked like half a circle, with a straight line on top. Josephine held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." She looked at the door. She looked at her hand. The same! "Five," she said. "That means five!"

"That is room five," said the librarian. "Your counting song is in there today." Josephine pushed the door open wide. Inside, kids sat on a rug. The lady kept singing. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Josephine sat down fast. She held up all ten fingers. "I know those words," she said. "Sing it again!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Julia walked into the band room. She saw a big piano. The piano had white keys and black keys. "Can I play it?" she asked. Mr. Bean nodded. "Sit here," he said.

Julia put her finger on a white key. It made a soft sound. She pressed a black key. It made a new sound. She wanted to make a song, but she felt upset. The white keys and the black keys mixed together. Her tune went all jumpy.

Then Julia had an idea. She used only her right hand on the black keys. She skipped over the white ones. Press, press, press. The black keys made sounds that fit together. It sounded like raindrops on the roof. Julia played it again. Press, press, press.

"That is a nice tune," said Mr. Bean. "What is its name?" Julia thought hard. "Raindrops," she said. "Its name is Raindrops." She gave the piano a little hug. Then she played her song one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Grandpa had a big poster on the wall. It showed all the letters. The big letters had shiny colors. Evan pointed at the big A. "A says ah," he said. "Like apple!"

Then Evan found a small book on the couch. He climbed up next to Grandpa. He looked at the first page. He saw a little round letter. "Grandpa! This is a new letter!" he said. "It is not on your wall!"

Grandpa smiled. He held up the poster. Evan looked at the wall. He looked at the book. The little letter looked small and shy. The wall letter was big and tall. Then Evan saw it. They both had the same bump and the same tail!

"Big A, small a," said Grandpa. "Same letter!"

"Big A, small a!" said Evan. "Same letter, same sound!" He said "ah" again. A feather floated down from Grandpa's pillow. "F!" said Evan. "That is F for feather!"

Grandpa laughed. "You are my letter finder," he said. Evan turned the page fast. "Next letter! Next letter!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Matthew ran up to the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. A lady named Miss Kay stood by the door. She had a big smile.

"Hello, Matthew," said Miss Kay. "Today you get your own library card."

She wrote his name on a small card. Matthew held it tight. His tooth felt loose when he grinned. He picked out a book about a red fire truck. Miss Kay put the book in a bag.

"You bring the book back next week," said Miss Kay.

"But how?" asked Matthew.

Miss Kay pointed to a little door on the side of the truck. "That is the return slot," she said. "It is a place to drop off books when you bring them back."

Matthew held his book close. He did not want to let it go. Miss Kay held his hand. "You can get a new book after," she said softly.

Matthew lifted the book. He dropped it in the slot. It slid down and was gone. Matthew waved at the slot. "Bye bye, book."

Miss Kay laughed and sang a little song. Then she handed him a book about a big yellow bus.

"New book," said Matthew. He hugged it all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Henry walked into his classroom. He held his daddy's hand. His bag felt heavy on his back. He saw blocks, paints, and a little red chair.

"I don't know anyone," said Henry. "Will school be fun alone?"

"Maybe you will find out," said Daddy with a smile.

At play time, Henry saw a boy by the window. The boy stood all alone. He held one green truck. Henry stood alone too, by the blocks. Two alone boys, and no friends yet.

Then Henry had an idea. He walked over to the truck boy. "My name is Henry," he said. "What is your name?"

"Sam," said the boy. "Want to touch my truck? It can carry the doctor car!"

"Two trucks," said Henry. "Yes!"

Henry and Sam pushed the trucks on the rug. Sam laughed when Henry made a loud truck noise. Henry laughed too. The teacher smiled at them.

At nap time, Henry waved at Sam. Sam waved back.

"Did school be fun alone?" Daddy asked later.

"No," said Henry. "It was fun with Sam!"

"Who is Sam?" asked Daddy.

"My friend," said Henry. "I asked him his name, and now we are friends forever!"

Henry showed Daddy his heavy bag. "Sam wants to come play on Saturday," he said. "Can he, can he?"

Daddy nodded. Henry cheered so loud that the doctor across the street looked up and waved. Henry waved back with both hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Art class was sunny and bright. Myles sat at the little table. He wanted to paint a boat, but he did not know how to make one.

Miss Ada gave him a paper with shapes. "Look at these," she said. There was a circle, a square, a triangle, and a rectangle. Myles touched the triangle. It felt pointy on his finger.

At snack time, Miss Ada cut Myles's sandwich. Each piece was a triangle. Myles counted the corners before he took a bite. One, two, three. "It has three corners," he said. His friend Poppy counted the sides of her piece. One, two, three. "Three sides too," she said.

Myles looked at his triangle sandwich. Then he looked at the paper. The triangle was pointy, just like a boat sail! He picked up his brush. He painted a square for the boat. He painted a triangle for the sail. He painted a big circle for the sun above it.

Miss Ada held the painting up. "What a fine sunny boat," she said. Myles hopped up from his chair. He clapped his hands. "I made a boat with shapes," he said. "My sail has three corners!" Poppy leaned over to look at the little white sail. "Mine will have three too," she said, picking up her brush.
